passage:
"You told your parents about me?" Tanuja set down her chai on the rooftop ledge.
"Not yet," Madhav said. "After placements."
"That's what you said after mid-sems."
"Tanu, it's complicated. They want someone who'll move to Dubai with me. Settle. You know."
"And I want to do rural medicine for five years. I told you that in our first week."
"I thought you'd change your mind."
"Did you want me to?"
Madhav looked at the water tank for a long time. "Honestly? Yes."
Tanuja's eyes filled, but her voice stayed level. "Then we want different lives, Madhav. You're not a bad person. We just want different lives."
"We could try —"
"We could try for two more years and then fight about it. I'd rather be sad now than bitter later."
He nodded slowly. "Can we at least finish this chai?"
She laughed, wetly. "Yes. This chai, we can finish."

qa.q: What does Tanuja want to do for five years?
qa.a: Rural medicine.

qa.q: What was Tanuja feeling when her eyes filled but her voice stayed level?
qa.a: Tanuja felt sad and hurt, yet clear and steady that their plans for life did not match.

qa.q: What did the couple handle wisely, and what might help each of them now?
qa.a: They named the real difference in life plans honestly instead of drifting for years; now each could lean on friends and give themselves time to grieve.

qa.q: What is it like for Madhav to admit he hoped Tanuja would change her mind?
qa.a: It is probably painful and embarrassing for Madhav, but saying it honestly lets both of them see the mismatch clearly.

grounding: A young couple talks honestly about different life values and chooses to part before resentment builds.

passage: I'm Trisha, and last winter, after Dev ended our two years with a text, I did everything wrong for a week. I reread our chats at 2 a.m. I checked who he was following. I skipped two lectures and told everyone I had a cold. My roommate Anjali didn't push. She just started leaving the door open when she went for her evening walk, and on the eighth day I went with her. We walked round the lake, barely talking. On day ten I muted Dev instead of watching him. On day fifteen I told Anjali the embarrassing part: I'd ignored how often he mocked my friends, because I was scared of being alone. Saying it aloud helped. It still hurt in March. But I began a list of what I'd actually want next time. Kindness to my people is at the top.

qa.q: How did Dev end the relationship?
qa.a: With a text.

qa.q: What was Trisha feeling during the first week after the breakup?
qa.a: Trisha felt heartbroken and restless, rereading chats at night and hiding the pain behind a pretend cold.

qa.q: Which steps helped Trisha recover?
qa.a: Walking with Anjali, muting Dev instead of watching him, and admitting what had been ignored all helped Trisha heal and think about values for next time.

qa.q: How might Anjali see her part in Trisha's recovery?
qa.a: Anjali chose patience over pushing, so she probably felt relieved and quietly glad when Trisha finally joined the walk.

grounding: A young adult looks back on recovering from a breakup and clarifying what to value in a future partner.

passage: Counselling centre, session note. Kamal (second year) came in two days after asking Pooja, a classmate, to go out with him. She said no, kindly and clearly. His first thought, he said, was to "keep trying till she sees it", and some friends told him to. We talked about what a clear no means, and how pushing would take away her comfort in the classroom they share. He said, "It feels like being told I'm not enough." We separated the two things: her choice, not his worth. By the end he decided to keep greetings normal in class, unfollow her for now, and spend fest week practising with his band. He looked lighter leaving. Follow-up after exams. — K. Rao, counsellor

qa.q: How did Pooja say no?
qa.a: Kindly and clearly.

qa.q: What was Kamal feeling about the rejection?
qa.a: Kamal felt hurt and inadequate, as if the no meant he was not enough.

qa.q: Why was the counsellor right to steer Kamal away from 'keep trying'?
qa.a: A clear no deserves respect; pushing would take away Pooja's comfort in class, while Kamal's plan protects both of them.

qa.q: What would change for Pooja if Kamal had followed his friends' advice?
qa.a: Pooja would likely feel uneasy and pressured in class, with her clear answer ignored instead of respected.

grounding: A counsellor's note shows a student handling romantic rejection by respecting the no and caring for himself.

passage: The last metro left at 11:10, and it was 10:48 when Arvind said, "Stay tonight? It's raining anyway." Shalini's stomach tightened. They had been together four months, and she liked him, liked how he remembered her exam dates. But she wasn't ready to stay over, and she had hoped it wouldn't come up tonight, with the rain loud on the tin shade and no time to think. Her phone buzzed: Sarita, her roommate. "Home by 11:40? Shall I wait up?" Shalini took a breath. "I'm not ready for staying over. I like you. It's just not yet." Arvind was quiet for a second, then picked up the umbrella. "Okay. Thanks for telling me straight. Come, we'll run." They reached the platform at 11:06, soaked. She texted Sarita: "On the metro. He was sweet about it."

qa.q: What time did the last metro leave?
What was Shalini feeling when Arvind asked her to stay?
qa.a: Shalini felt anxious and pressured by the rain and the ticking clock, though she liked Arvind and simply wasn't ready.

qa.q: What could others learn from how both of them handled it?
qa.a: Shalini stated her boundary clearly and kindly, and Arvind accepted it at once, thanked her and helped her catch the metro.

qa.q: How might Sarita see the evening from her side?
qa.a: Sarita cared enough to offer to wait up, so reading 'He was sweet about it' would likely leave her relieved.

grounding: Under time pressure, a young woman states a boundary about staying over and her partner respects it.

passage: The student health centre on the third floor smelled of phenyl and the marigolds from someone's puja. Hansa had walked past its door twice before Zeenat linked arms and steered her in. "You said you wanted proper information, not internet rubbish," Zeenat whispered. Hansa's ears burned. She and Nikhil had been together a year and were talking about becoming intimate, and she wanted to understand protection and testing before anything happened. The nurse, reading glasses on a chain, didn't blink. She closed the door, gave Hansa leaflets, answered every question plainly, then asked one of her own: "Have you two talked about what each of you is comfortable with, and that either of you can stop anytime?" Hansa shook her head. "Start there," the nurse said. On the stairs down, Hansa laughed shakily. "That was the least awkward awkward thing ever."

qa.q: Where was the student health centre?
qa.a: On the third floor.

qa.q: What does Hansa walking past the door twice suggest?
qa.a: Hansa felt embarrassed and nervous about asking, even though she wanted proper information.

qa.q: What was wise about the nurse's question, and what should Hansa's next step be?
qa.a: It turned the focus to open talk with Nikhil about comfort and the right to stop anytime; Hansa's next step is that conversation.

qa.q: How might Zeenat feel on the way down the stairs?
qa.a: Zeenat would likely feel relieved and glad she nudged Hansa in, seeing Hansa laugh after something so hard to start.

grounding: A young woman, supported by a friend, seeks reliable sexual-health information and is guided to talk about consent first.

passage:
"Okay, pretend I'm Sameer," Pooja said, flopping onto the hostel bed. "Go."
Mahima laughed nervously. "This is so silly."
"Last time you went quiet when you felt rushed, and then felt bad for days. So. Practice."
Mahima breathed out. "Sameer, I really like you. I want us to go slow. If I say stop, or go quiet, can you check with me?"
Pooja, in a deep voice: "What if I think you're just shy?"
"Then ask. Don't guess."
"Wow. Okay. That was clear." Pooja dropped the voice. "How do you feel?"
"Shaky. But like the words exist now."
"And if he sulks about it?"
Mahima picked at the blanket. "Then that tells me something about him, doesn't it?"
"It does." Pooja squeezed her hand. "You deserve someone who's glad you said it."

qa.q: Who did Pooja pretend to be?
qa.a: Sameer.

qa.q: How did Mahima feel after saying the words aloud?
qa.a: Mahima felt shaky but more confident, as if the words now existed for the real conversation.

qa.q: What makes Mahima's rehearsed sentence a good boundary statement?
qa.a: It is warm but clear: it says she likes him, wants to go slow, and asks him to check in rather than guess.

qa.q: Why might Pooja push Mahima to practise?
qa.a: Pooja saw Mahima feel bad for days after going quiet last time, so practising is a caring way to help her find her voice.

grounding: Two friends rehearse how to state a boundary and ask a partner to check for consent rather than guess.

passage: Kunal's first week at the Bengaluru office, and his phone showed nine missed calls from Ma by lunch. Binita called the way she breathed: after every meal, before every bus. Today the office network was down, his manager wanted a report by four, and the phone was at seven percent. At 3:40 it buzzed again. He stepped into the stairwell. "Ma, I'm fine. I'm in the middle of work." "You didn't answer! I thought something happened." He heard the fear under the scolding and softened. "I know. Can we do this: I'll message you when I reach the office and when I leave, and we'll talk properly every night at nine? If anything's wrong, you'll be the first I call." Silence. Then, "Nine o'clock. Not nine-thirty." He smiled. "Nine." The phone died as he walked back in; he finished the report at 3:58.

qa.q: How many missed calls from Ma did Kunal have by lunch?
qa.a: Nine missed calls.

qa.q: What was Kunal feeling when he stepped into the stairwell?
qa.a: Kunal felt stressed and pulled two ways by the deadline, the dying phone and a worried mother, but softened when he heard her fear.

qa.q: Why is Kunal's offer a healthy boundary rather than a rejection?
qa.a: It keeps contact predictable, with messages on arrival and departure and a nightly call, while protecting work time and reassuring Ma.

qa.q: How does Binita experience Kunal's move to a new city?
qa.a: Binita seems frightened whenever he doesn't answer, so the new routine gives her reassurance without constant calls.

grounding: A young man in his first job sets a caring boundary on his mother's calls, moving towards an adult relationship.

passage: On Sunday morning in their Dadar flat, Pranav waited until Papa had finished the newspaper crossword. "Papa, two things." Siddharth looked up, pen still in hand. "First, I'll take Dadi to her Thursday check-ups from now. My classes end early that day." His father blinked. "You? You get lost in hospitals." "I got lost once, when I was twelve." "Hm. And second?" "Please knock before coming into my room." The pen went still. For a moment Pranav feared he had hurt him. Then Siddharth said gruffly, "I said the same to my father at your age. He sulked for a week." "Are you going to sulk?" "Maybe two days." On Thursday Pranav brought Dadi home with her reports in a neat folder. That evening there was a knock at his door, a little too loud, a little awkward. He grinned. "Come in."

qa.q: On which day are Dadi's check-ups?
qa.a: On Thursday.

qa.q: What was Pranav worried about when the pen went still?
qa.a: Pranav was anxious that asking Papa to knock had hurt him.

qa.q: What made Pranav's request work well?
qa.a: Pranav paired a boundary with a grown-up responsibility, taking Dadi to check-ups, so it felt like partnership rather than pushing Papa away.

qa.q: How does Siddharth experience being asked to knock?
qa.a: Siddharth feels a little hurt and awkward, but remembering his own youth helps him accept it with humour, even if the first knock is too loud.

grounding: A young man in Mumbai takes on family responsibility and asks for privacy, and his father adjusts.

passage:
"Ammi, sit. I made the chai today."
"Since when do you make chai?" Ammi sat, suspicious.
"Since my first salary." Parveen pushed an envelope across. "For the electricity and gas. Every month."
"Beta, keep your money."
"I'll keep some. But I live here. I want to pay my share."
Ammi turned the envelope over. "Your Abbu will say I allowed it."
"Then I'll tell him myself. And Ammi, one more thing. When Khala asks about rishtas for me, can you say, 'Ask Parveen'?"
"You'll embarrass me."
"I'll be polite. I just want to be asked, not discussed."
Ammi was quiet a long while. "When did you grow up?"
"Somewhere between college and this chai."
Ammi laughed and wiped her eye with the corner of her dupatta. "Fine. But the chai needs more ginger."

qa.q: What is the envelope for?
qa.a: The electricity and gas, every month.

qa.q: How can you tell Parveen was nervous about this talk?
qa.a: Making chai first and preparing the envelope suggest Parveen was anxious and planned carefully, wanting to be taken seriously.

qa.q: Why does Parveen's request about rishtas work as a boundary?
qa.a: It is specific and polite: Parveen asks to be consulted directly rather than discussed, and offers to speak to Abbu too.

qa.q: How does Ammi see Parveen by the end of the talk?
qa.a: Ammi sees Parveen as an adult now, asking 'When did you grow up?', and seems moved and proud even while teasing about the ginger.

grounding: A young adult begins contributing at home and asks to be consulted on her own marriage talks, reshaping the relationship with her mother.

passage: Every year at the Puja fair in their village near Bishnupur, Anirban and Jatin had eaten jilipi from the same stall. This year Jatin was in Surat, working night shifts at a textile unit, and Anirban was home from college alone. Their chats had shrunk to thumbs-up. On the second evening Anirban stood at the stall and felt oddly heavy. Then he recorded a voice note: the drums, the stall owner shouting, his own voice saying, "Your share is going cold, bhai." Twenty minutes later Jatin replied, voice cracking with laughter and tiredness: "I can smell it from here." They talked for forty minutes during Jatin's break. Before hanging up, they fixed something small: a voice note every Sunday, even thirty seconds, and a proper call on every festival.

qa.q: Where was Jatin working?
qa.a: In Surat, on night shifts at a textile unit.

qa.q: What was Anirban feeling at the jilipi stall on the second evening?
qa.a: Anirban felt heavy and lonely, missing Jatin at a place the two had always shared.

qa.q: Why is the Sunday voice note a realistic way to stay close?
qa.a: It is small enough to fit around night shifts and college, so it can last, with festival calls for longer talks.

qa.q: What was it like for Jatin to receive the voice note?
qa.a: Jatin, tired from night shifts, was moved and amused, laughing that he could smell the jilipi from Surat.

grounding: Two village friends separated by work and college agree on small regular contact to keep their friendship alive.

passage: For three Saturdays running, Tariq cancelled. First a double shift at the café in Leeds, then a group project, then a flu. Each time Alejandro replied "no worries 👍" from Valencia, and each time the thumbs-up felt a little colder. They had shared a flat for two years at university; now they barely shared a sentence. On a Sunday night Tariq finally wrote the message he had been avoiding: "I keep promising big calls and then bailing. Can we do small instead? Fifteen minutes while I walk to work on Tuesdays?" Alejandro's reply took an hour. "Honestly I thought you were drifting on purpose. Tuesdays. I'll be making lunch, you'll hear pans." The first Tuesday call lasted twenty-two minutes. Tariq arrived at work late and didn't mind at all.

qa.q: Where does Alejandro live now?
qa.a: In Valencia.

qa.q: What was Tariq feeling each time the thumbs-up arrived?
qa.a: Tariq felt guilty and uneasy, sensing the friendship cooling with every cancellation.

qa.q: Why was Tariq's new plan more likely to work than the big calls?
qa.a: Fifteen minutes during an existing walk fits around shifts and projects, so it is a promise small enough to keep.

qa.q: How had Alejandro been seeing Tariq's cancellations?
qa.a: Alejandro thought Tariq was drifting on purpose, so the cheerful replies probably hid hurt and disappointment.

grounding: Two former flatmates in different countries replace cancelled big calls with a small weekly habit.

passage: When the rota changed at the call centre in Gurugram, Dilnaz moved to nights and Tushar stayed on days. For two years they had shared the 1 p.m. canteen table and grumbled about the same customers. Now their only overlap was the ten minutes at shift change, when he was leaving and she was badging in, both too tired to talk. After a month Dilnaz noticed she no longer knew what was going on in his life. So she stuck a note inside his locker: "Samosa + 10 minutes, Friday 9:50 pm, bench by the gate?" On Friday he was there with two samosas and a flask of tea. They didn't solve anything. He told her about his sister's wedding plans; she told him about the man who had sung her a song on a complaint call. It became their Friday. Some weeks it was only five minutes.

qa.q: Where did Dilnaz suggest they meet?
qa.a: At the bench by the gate.

qa.q: How might Dilnaz have felt noticing she no longer knew what was going on in Tushar's life?
qa.a: Dilnaz probably felt a little lonely and sad, sensing the friendship slipping away because of the new shifts.

qa.q: Why did the locker note work where tired chats at shift change didn't?
qa.a: It set a small, specific time and place, Friday at the bench with samosas, so they met on purpose instead of hoping to catch each other.

qa.q: How might Tushar have felt finding the note?
qa.a: Tushar probably felt pleased and valued, since he turned up with samosas and a flask.

grounding: Two colleagues split by a shift change keep their friendship going with a short, fixed weekly meeting.

passage: Bihu fell on a Saturday, and Sunaina's Pune hostel had emptied for the long weekend. The mess was shut, her roommate was in Nashik, and the rain had knocked out the corridor lights. She ate instant noodles on her bed and scrolled through photos of her cousins in mekhelas back in Jorhat until her throat hurt. The photography club had posted "rainy walk, anyone welcome" for five o'clock. She almost didn't go. She put on her damp shoes anyway. Only four people came. One, Tushar, a second-year from Manipur, was also skipping home because tickets were too dear. They photographed puddles and a dog asleep under a scooter. At the tea stall afterwards he said, "First year, I spent every festival crying on the phone." Sunaina laughed, surprised. "Only first year?" "Mostly." They planned next Saturday's walk.

qa.q: How many people came to the rainy walk?
qa.a: Only four people.

qa.q: What was Sunaina feeling while scrolling the photos of her cousins?
qa.a: Sunaina felt homesick and lonely in the empty hostel on a festival weekend, holding back tears.

qa.q: What small step turned the weekend, and what could Sunaina keep doing?
qa.a: Going to the open club walk despite the rain; Sunaina could keep joining regular, low-pressure group activities like next Saturday's walk.

qa.q: How might Tushar see Sunaina's first-year loneliness?
qa.a: Tushar recognises it from his own first year of crying on the phone, so he sees it as normal and passing, not a sign something is wrong with her.

grounding: Alone on a festival weekend far from home, a student pushes herself to join a club walk and finds belonging.

passage: Ujjwal's PG room in Madhapur had a window facing another building's wall. For six weeks after starting his first job in Hyderabad, his routine was office, cab, dinner eaten standing at that window, and a call home where Ma asked if he had made friends yet. "Yes, yes," he lied. At work he ate lunch at his desk. One Friday, Swati from the next team stopped by. "We play cricket in the colony park on Sundays. Terrible cricket. We need an eleventh." He almost said he was busy. Instead he asked what time. On Sunday he dropped two catches and made twelve runs, and afterwards six sweaty strangers argued with him about the best biryani in the city. That night, when Ma asked the usual question, he said, "I'm starting to," and it was true.

qa.q: What did Ujjwal's PG window face?
qa.a: Another building's wall.

qa.q: Why did Ujjwal lie to Ma about making friends?
qa.a: Ujjwal felt lonely and a little ashamed, and didn't want Ma to worry.

qa.q: What could Ujjwal do to keep building belonging after that Sunday?
qa.a: Ujjwal could keep turning up to the weekly game and start eating lunch with Swati's team instead of alone at the desk.

qa.q: How might Swati see the invitation?
qa.a: Swati probably thought of it as a small, casual ask, without knowing how much it would mean to a lonely newcomer.

grounding: A young man lonely in a new city accepts a colleague's invitation and starts to belong.

passage:
"You're cooking dal at midnight again," Thomas said, leaning in the kitchen doorway.
Neelam jumped. "Sorry. Is it the smell?"
"No, it smells amazing. It's more that you're always in here alone at midnight."
She stirred. "It's morning at home. Mummy calls around now."
"And then?"
"And then I sit in my room, and everyone's asleep in both countries."
Thomas was quiet. "I moved to Glasgow from Orkney. First term I didn't speak to anyone for nine days. I counted."
"Nine?"
"Nine. Then Morag from upstairs dragged me to the hill-walking society."
"I don't walk hills."
"Nobody really does. We walk to the café at the bottom and talk." He paused. "Saturday? Bring some of that dal. They'll love you forever."
Neelam laughed for the first time that week. "Fine. But you're carrying the pot."

qa.q: How many days did Thomas go without speaking to anyone?
qa.a: Nine days.

qa.q: What was Neelam feeling when she said everyone's asleep in both countries?
qa.a: Neelam felt lonely and cut off, belonging fully to neither place at that hour.

qa.q: What makes Thomas's invitation a good first step for Neelam?
qa.a: It is specific and low-pressure, a Saturday walk with an easy role of bringing dal, which gives her a way in.

qa.q: How might Thomas see Neelam's midnight cooking?
qa.a: Thomas recognises his own lonely first term in it, so he sees it as a sign she needs company, not a nuisance.

grounding: A lonely international student is invited into a university group by a flatmate who once felt the same.

passage: Irawati, you think four girls in one flat is hard? Let your Rajni Masi tell you about Room 14. We were three in a hostel room built for two, in Lucknow, 1998. Sushma kept her lamp on till two, Jaya left dishes under the bed, and I, madam, used everybody's soap. For a month we sulked and stuck notes on the mirror. Then one night Jaya's dishes grew a smell even I couldn't ignore, and I shouted. Jaya cried. And Sushma, the quiet one, said, "Let's each say one thing that bothers us and one thing we'll change. No shouting." So we did. Lamp off at midnight. Dishes washed by morning. Soap, my own. And we pooled for a kettle, everybody the same share. It wasn't perfect. But Jaya is still my dearest friend. Sit, I'll tell you what she said about my soap.

qa.q: What was Jaya's habit that caused trouble?
qa.a: Leaving dishes under the bed.

qa.q: How did Jaya feel when Rajni shouted?
qa.a: Jaya felt hurt and upset and cried, after a month of tension burst out as shouting.

qa.q: What was the turning point in Room 14, and why did it work?
qa.a: Sushma's rule of one complaint and one change each, with no shouting, turned blame into fair, specific agreements everyone could keep.

qa.q: How might Sushma have seen the month of sulking and mirror notes?
qa.a: Sushma, the quiet one, probably felt tired and uneasy with the tension, which may be why she proposed a calmer way to talk.

grounding: An aunt tells how three hostel roommates turned sulking into fair agreements about chores, space and shared costs.

passage: The electricity bill arrived in the hottest week of May: nearly double. Kalyani stuck it to the fridge with a mango magnet and waited. Deepak, who worked from home and ran the cooler in his room all day, saw it first and went quiet. Hema, the third flatmate, was away at her sister's. Kalyani had rehearsed an angry speech in the shower. Instead, at dinner, she said, "The bill doubled. I'm not blaming anyone, but splitting it three ways doesn't feel fair when we use it so differently." Deepak rubbed his neck. "It's the cooler. I can't work in forty-two degrees." "I get that," she said. "Can we note the meter every evening for a week and agree a fairer split once Hema's back?" He thought, then nodded. They messaged Hema together straight away, so she wouldn't come home to a deal already made.

qa.q: How much had the electricity bill gone up?
qa.a: It had nearly doubled.

qa.q: What was Deepak feeling when he saw the bill and went quiet?
qa.a: Deepak likely felt guilty and a bit defensive, knowing the cooler he ran all day was probably the cause.

qa.q: What made Kalyani's approach at dinner fair?
qa.a: She named the problem without blaming, accepted Deepak's need to work in the heat, and suggested measuring before deciding.

qa.q: What would change for Hema if the others had decided without her?
qa.a: Hema would come back to a deal made without her voice and might feel left out or resentful, even if the split was fair.

grounding: In a heatwave, flatmates negotiate a fair way to share a doubled bill, including the absent flatmate.

passage: By the third week in their Andheri flat, the bathroom had become a silent war. Ritu cleaned it on Sundays. Vishal said he would "do it next time", and next time never came. Rather than write another sarcastic note, Ritu waited until he was making his evening omelette. "Can we talk chores for five minutes?" He flipped the omelette, wary. "Is this about the bathroom?" "Partly. I've done it four Sundays. I'm starting to resent you, and I don't want to." Vishal winced. "I hate cleaning it. I'd rather do the grocery runs, the gas bookings and the dishes every night." Ritu considered. Dishes every night was more work than one bathroom a week. "Deal, if the dishes really happen. Check in next Sunday?" They wrote it on a sheet taped inside a kitchen cupboard, where guests wouldn't see.

qa.q: How many Sundays had Ritu cleaned the bathroom?
qa.a: Four Sundays.

qa.q: What was Ritu feeling before raising the chores?
qa.a: Ritu was starting to feel resentful about doing the bathroom alone, and worried that the resentment would sour things between them.

qa.q: Why is a check-in next Sunday a good part of the deal?
qa.a: It gives both a chance to see whether the swap is working and adjust fairly before resentment builds again.

qa.q: How does Vishal see the chore swap?
qa.a: Vishal is relieved to trade the task he hates for ones he'd rather do, and his wince suggests he knows he had been unfair.

grounding: Two flatmates in Mumbai turn a silent chore conflict into a fair trade with a check-in.

subtype: Recognizing Warning Signs & Seeking Professional Help
passage:
Week one of finals prep. Keerthana stopped going to the evening badminton she had played for three years. "No time," she told Kamal. She slept eleven hours on Sunday and still woke tired.
Three weeks later. She hadn't answered her mother's calls in four days. The notes she used to colour-code sat unopened. When Kamal knocked with dinner, she said through the door, "What's the point? I'll fail anyway." Kamal didn't leave. He sat outside and said, "This isn't laziness. It's been weeks. Will you come with me to the counselling centre tomorrow at ten? I'll wait outside."
Five weeks later. Keerthana had seen the counsellor twice and a doctor once. Some days she was still tired. But she had called her mother back, and on Friday she picked up her racket and played one slow game.

qa.q: What sport had Keerthana played for three years?
qa.a: Badminton.

qa.q: What does 'What's the point? I'll fail anyway' suggest about how Keerthana felt?
qa.a: It suggests Keerthana felt hopeless and exhausted, not just stressed, after weeks of pulling away from people.

qa.q: What did Kamal get right, and how could other friends do the same?
qa.a: He named that it had lasted weeks, didn't call it laziness, and offered to go with her at a set time; friends can make getting help concrete like that.

qa.q: How might Keerthana's mother have felt during the four days of unanswered calls?
qa.a: Her mother was probably worried and anxious, unsure what was wrong, and likely relieved when Keerthana finally called back.

grounding: Over weeks, a student's exhaustion and withdrawal are noticed by a friend, and she gets professional help early.

subtype: Recognizing Warning Signs & Seeking Professional Help
passage: Tenzin, you keep saying you're "just tired". Let me, your old Urmila Didi from the ward, tell you something. When I was twenty-two I was a staff nurse in my first year, taking double shifts because I thought saying no meant I was weak. For two months I stopped eating proper meals. I stopped going to my friend Leela's for Sunday lunch. I cried in the linen room and told myself everyone does. One morning I stood at the trolley and couldn't remember why I was there. My matron, a stern woman called Mrs Gomes, took me into her office. She didn't scold. She said, "This has gone on too long. You'll see the staff doctor today, and I'm taking you off doubles." I was ashamed then. Now I think she saved my career. So when you say "just tired" for the third month, I hear my younger self.

qa.q: Where did Urmila cry?
qa.a: In the linen room.

qa.q: What was young Urmila feeling when Mrs Gomes took her into the office?

qa.q: What was the turning point in Urmila's story, and why did it matter?

subtype: Recognizing Warning Signs & Seeking Professional Help
passage: Vikas had worn the same grey hoodie for a week. In the lab he stared at the oscilloscope while Sabina did both parts of the experiment. "Sorry," he kept saying. "Just tired." He had said that since September. It was November. Sabina had noticed other things: he'd left the hostel football group, he skipped meals, and once he said, flatly, that nothing felt worth trying anymore. After lab she walked him to the student wellness centre. The receptionist said the next counselling slot was in twelve days; exams started in five. Vikas turned to leave, shoulders dropping. Sabina asked, "Is there anyone he can talk to sooner?" The receptionist gave them the college's free support line and said a duty counsellor saw urgent cases that week. Vikas called from the bench outside, with Sabina beside him, and got a slot for Thursday.

qa.q: How many days away was the next counselling slot?
qa.a: Twelve days.

qa.q: What does Vikas saying nothing felt worth trying suggest?
qa.a: It suggests Vikas felt hopeless and drained, well beyond ordinary tiredness after months of withdrawing.

qa.q: What did Sabina do when the first answer was 'twelve days', and why did it help?
qa.a: Sabina asked whether anyone could help sooner, which uncovered the support line and the duty counsellor, so help came that week instead of after exams.

qa.q: What is it like for Sabina to watch Vikas over these months?
qa.a: Sabina has been carrying the lab work and noticing worrying signs, so she likely felt concerned and then relieved when he got a Thursday slot.

grounding: Despite a long wait for counselling during exams, a student's warning signs are acted on and he gets help early.

passage: Behind the counter of her father's hardware shop in Karad, Lakshmi kept her phone under the ledger. The card game started as ten minutes between customers. Win a little, feel bright. Lose a little, play one more to win it back. By July she was topping up from the shop's cash drawer and writing the gaps in pencil so she could "fix them later". Jahnavi, her school friend, came in for nails and saw her hands shaking as a round ended. "Lakshmi, you're not even looking at me." That night Lakshmi added up the pencil gaps and felt sick. She told Jahnavi first, then, with Jahnavi sitting beside her, her father. He was silent a long time. Then he said, "We'll fix the drawer together. And you'll see someone." Next morning they went to the counsellor at the district hospital, and Lakshmi deleted the game in the waiting room.

qa.q: Where did Lakshmi keep her phone?
qa.a: Under the ledger.

qa.q: What was Lakshmi feeling when she added up the pencil gaps?
qa.a: Lakshmi felt sick with shame and fear once she saw how much had gone from the drawer.

qa.q: What steps helped Lakshmi start to break the loop?
qa.a: Telling Jahnavi and then her father that same night, going to the counsellor at the district hospital, and deleting the game removed the secrecy and the easy access.

qa.q: How might Lakshmi's father have felt during his long silence?
qa.a: He was probably shocked and hurt, then worried for her, choosing to fix things together rather than only punish.

grounding: In a small town, a young woman caught in a gambling loop tells her friend and father and starts getting help.

passage: In Jana's first year at university in Brno, every evening ended the same way. A beer to "switch off" after lectures, then two, then messages she regretted in the morning. By spring she needed a drink before any seminar where she had to speak. One Sunday Ada, her flatmate, found the empty bottles in the recycling and didn't lecture. She asked, "When did it stop being fun?" Jana opened her mouth to joke and couldn't. "Maybe November," she said. "I don't know how to talk in class without it anymore." That frightened her more than any hangover. That evening, with Ada beside her, she called the student support line. The adviser listened, told her she had done the right thing by calling, and booked her with a counsellor for Monday. Ada offered evening swims together instead of the drinks.

qa.q: Where did Ada find the empty bottles?
qa.a: In the recycling.

qa.q: Why was Jana frightened by her own answer to Ada?
qa.a: Jana felt frightened realising she no longer knew how to speak in class without drinking, a sign the habit had become a need.

qa.q: What makes this a realistic start to leaving the loop?
qa.a: Calling the support line the same day brought in a professional, the counsellor appointment adds ongoing help, and swims with Ada replace the evening habit.

qa.q: How might Ada have felt asking 'When did it stop being fun?'
qa.a: Ada was probably worried but careful, choosing a gentle question over a lecture so Jana could answer honestly.

grounding: A student abroad recognises a drinking dependence loop when a flatmate asks gently, and seeks help that day.

passage: The attendance notice said sixty-one percent. Harsha folded it into quarters before walking into the campus wellness centre. Ishita, a final-year volunteer at the front desk, noticed his red eyes and offered him water while he waited. "I play one match at night to relax," he told her, almost defensively. "Then it's four a.m. Then I miss the nine o'clock class. Then I feel rubbish, so I play again." Ishita nodded. Advice wasn't her job. She wrote down the loop he had just described, word for word, and handed it to him. "Tell the counsellor exactly this. It's clearer than most people manage." Inside, the counsellor listened, and together they made a plan: the console left at his cousin's flat for the semester, a sports club at night, and weekly check-ins. Harsha came out and gave Ishita a small, embarrassed thumbs-up.

qa.q: What attendance did the notice show?
qa.a: Sixty-one percent.

qa.q: What was Harsha feeling while describing the loop?
qa.a: Harsha felt defensive and ashamed, feeling rubbish after missed classes yet pulled back into playing.

qa.q: Which parts of the plan target the loop directly?
qa.a: Leaving the console at his cousin's flat removes the trigger, the night-time sports club fills that slot, and weekly check-ins keep him on track.

qa.q: How might Ishita feel seeing the embarrassed thumbs-up?
qa.a: Ishita would likely feel quietly glad that writing down his own words helped him speak to the counsellor.

grounding: At a campus wellness centre, a student describes his gaming loop and makes a plan with a counsellor to exit it.

passage: I'm Baljeet, Harish's roommate, and I still don't fully know what went on in his head that week. Our whole batch had a system: one person marked proxy attendance for five friends, turn by turn. Harish's turn came on Monday. He sat with the attendance sheet in the corridor for a long time. Then he signed only his own name and walked in. The others were furious. Someone called him "the saint". At dinner I asked him why. He shrugged and said, "I just decided I don't want my name on anything untrue. Not even small things." He didn't lecture anyone. He just stopped. By the end of the month two others had stopped too, though nobody said it out loud. I still sign for myself only, and I'm not sure whether that's his influence or mine.

qa.q: How many friends did one person mark proxy attendance for?
qa.a: Five friends.

qa.q: What might Harish have been feeling as he sat with the sheet for a long time?
qa.a: Harish was probably torn between loyalty to the batch and not wanting his name on anything untrue, and perhaps nervous about the anger to come.

qa.q: What made Harish's stand effective without a lecture?
qa.a: He simply acted on his value by signing only his own name, which let others choose for themselves; two later stopped too.

qa.q: How does Baljeet see Harish's choice, without knowing his inner thoughts?
qa.a: Baljeet seems curious and quietly impressed, noticing the calm reply and that others followed, while admitting not fully knowing what was in Harish's head.

grounding: A roommate describes a student who quietly refuses his batch's proxy-attendance system to stay true to his own value.

passage:
January. Sabina's cousins had all done MBAs, and at the family lunch her uncle said, "You'll apply this year, of course." Her college friends were planning a Goa trip she couldn't afford and didn't want. She said yes to both and felt hollow on the bus home.
February. In the library, her friend Irawati slid over a blank page. "Write five things you'd still do if nobody clapped." Sabina wrote: teaching kids to read, honesty, time with Nani, learning Urdu, staying out of debt. The MBA wasn't on it. Neither was Goa.
April. She told her uncle she was applying for a two-year teaching fellowship instead. He frowned and said she would regret it. She told her friends she'd skip the trip and meet them for chai when they got back. Her hands shook both times. That night, filling in the fellowship form, she felt steady.

qa.q: What did Irawati ask Sabina to write?
qa.a: Five things she'd still do if nobody clapped.

qa.q: How did Sabina's feelings change from the January bus ride to April?
qa.a: In January Sabina felt hollow after saying yes to everyone; by April, though her hands shook, she felt steady acting on her own values.

qa.q: Why was Irawati's question a useful tool?
qa.a: It separated what Sabina valued from what earned approval, making it clear the MBA and the trip weren't really hers.

qa.q: How might Sabina's uncle see her choice?
qa.a: Her uncle frowns and predicts regret, so he probably sees it as a risky break from the family's path, perhaps out of worry for her.

grounding: Over months, a young woman works out her own values and turns down both family and peer expectations.

passage: Kiran, you asked how anyone knows what they stand for. I'll tell you about the winter I was twenty-one, in Madurai. A rumour went round our street about my friend Salim's family, nasty and untrue. My cricket friends stopped talking to him. My own uncle said, "Keep your distance, Karthik, for your sister's sake." For a week I did. I crossed the road when I saw Salim. At night I hated myself. Then Salim's father had a fall, and I heard about it from the milkman. I went to the hospital and sat with Salim on that bench till morning. My friends didn't speak to me for two months. My uncle shouted. But that bench is where I found my first non-negotiable: I don't drop a friend because a crowd says so. You'll find yours, Kiran, probably on some uncomfortable bench of your own.

qa.q: How did Karthik hear about Salim's father's fall?
qa.a: From the milkman.

qa.q: What was Karthik feeling during the week he avoided Salim?
qa.a: Karthik felt guilty and hated himself at night for crossing the road to avoid a friend.

qa.q: What was the turning point for Karthik, and what did it cost?
qa.a: Going to sit with Salim at the hospital; it cost two months of silence from friends and his uncle's anger, but it fixed his first non-negotiable.

qa.q: How might Salim have felt seeing Karthik arrive at the hospital?
qa.a: Salim, already shut out because of the rumour, would likely have felt relieved and deeply grateful that a friend came back when it mattered.

grounding: An older man tells how, at twenty-one, he chose loyalty to a wronged friend over his peers and family.

passage: Imran walked out of the fourth-floor interview room knowing he had blown it. He had frozen on a basic database question he had practised a hundred times. In the lift his mind started its usual speech: Useless. Everyone else manages. Abbu spent his savings on your course for this. Outside it was pouring, the auto drivers wanted double, and his phone showed a message from Ojas: "How did it go??" He typed "terrible, I'm an idiot" and stopped. Ojas had failed three interviews last year, and Imran had never once called him an idiot. He deleted it and wrote instead: "Froze on joins. Annoying, because I know them. Going to redo ten join problems tonight and ask HR for feedback." He stood under the bus shelter, rain dripping down his neck, and felt his chest loosen a little.

qa.q: Which question did Imran freeze on?
qa.a: A basic database question he had practised a hundred times.

qa.q: What was Imran feeling in the lift?
qa.a: Imran felt ashamed and guilty, calling himself useless and thinking of Abbu's savings.

qa.q: How is Imran's second message better than 'I'm an idiot'?
qa.a: It names the specific mistake, admits it is annoying, and sets concrete fixes like ten join problems and asking for feedback, which is accountable without cruelty.

qa.q: How might Ojas react to Imran's second message?
qa.a: Ojas, who failed three interviews last year, would likely feel reassured that Imran is coping and might offer to practise together.

grounding: After a failed interview on a rainy day, a young man swaps harsh self-talk for the kind, practical words he'd give a friend.

passage: The result page loaded slowly on the library computer at her Kolkata college, and there it was: Kashish had failed Statistics, the only red among six subjects. She logged out and sat very still. The voice in her head was her own but sounded like a stranger: You always do this. You're lazy. You'll never finish. On the tram home she opened a note on her phone to list everything wrong with herself. Her friend Uma called instead. "I saw your face in the library. Speak." Kashish recited the list. Uma listened, then said, "Now say it the way you'd say it to me if I'd failed." Kashish was quiet a long moment. "I'd say you missed four weeks when Nani was in hospital, and you still passed five. Book the supplementary exam and ask Ma'am for the missed notes." Uma said, "Right. Now say that to yourself."

qa.q: How many subjects did Kashish have?
qa.a: Six subjects.

qa.q: What was Kashish feeling when she logged out and sat very still?
qa.a: Kashish felt shocked and ashamed, with a harsh inner voice calling her lazy.

qa.q: What did Uma's question help Kashish do?
qa.a: It let Kashish speak to herself as she would to a friend, naming the real cause, Nani's hospital stay, and practical steps like the supplementary exam and notes.

qa.q: How might Uma have felt seeing Kashish's face in the library?
qa.a: Uma was probably worried and wanted to help straight away, which is why the call came instead of waiting.

grounding: A college student in Kolkata turns harsh self-criticism after a failed subject into kind, accountable self-talk with a friend's help.

passage:
"I sent the client the old figures," Indu said, staring into her cold coffee. "The old ones. To the whole mailing list."
Manoj leaned on the pantry counter. "Okay. And?"
"And I'm the most careless person alive. Sir will think I'm useless. I think I'm useless."
"Stop. What actually happened?"
"I had two files with the same name. I picked the wrong one."
"So, one mistake with a clear cause."
"One mistake the whole client saw."
"And what did you do after?"
Indu sighed. "Sent a correction in ten minutes. Told Sir before he found out."
"That's what a responsible person does. Not a useless one."
"It doesn't feel like it."
"It won't, for a day. So what changes?"
She sat up slightly. "Date in every file name. And I check the attachment before anything goes to a client."
"See? That's the useful voice. The other one just shouts."
Indu almost smiled.

qa.q: Why did Indu pick the wrong file?
qa.a: She had two files with the same name.

qa.q: What was Indu feeling as she stared into her cold coffee?
qa.a: Indu felt ashamed and was harsh with herself, calling herself useless after the client saw the mistake.

qa.q: Which of Manoj's questions helped most, and why?
qa.a: 'What actually happened?' and 'So what changes?' moved Indu from self-attack to a clear cause and a fix, like dates in file names.

qa.q: How might Sir see Indu's handling of the mistake?
qa.a: Sir would likely see responsibility in a correction within ten minutes and being told before he found out, not carelessness.

grounding: A young employee, helped by a colleague, replaces self-attack after a work mistake with accountable, supportive self-talk.
